name: Kaupaloki
powers: Brings success and fair fortune in buying and selling.
description: Kaupaloki, the trade-luck stave of the Huld manuscript, inscribed for success in buying and selling. Drawn or carved by merchants, it was meant to bring profit and good dealings in the market. It belongs to the practical folk magic of Iceland's seafaring trade, where a stave for fair fortune in commerce was worth its weight in cargo.
source: Huld manuscript (Lbs 4626 8vo, 1860)

name: Hymir's Cauldron
powers: Deep enough to brew ale for all the gods at a single feast.
description: The great cauldron of the giant Hymir, fetched by Thor and Týr so that the gods could brew ale enough for a feast. Hymiskviða says it was a mile deep; when Hymir refused to give it up, Thor took the kettle and carried it away. The same visit produced the god's famous fishing for the Midgard serpent Jörmungandr.
source: Poetic Edda (Hymiskviða)

name: Knotted Rope Charm
maker: Tied by a 'wise' seller or Sami sorcerer
powers: Untying a knot raises wind; the third knot calls a storm.
description: A rope or cord with three knots, tied by a 'wise' seller and sold to sailors as a wind charm. Untying the first knot raised a gentle wind, the second a stronger breeze, and the third a storm, so prudent captains kept the third knot tied. The three-knotted wind cord is documented in Nordic and Sami maritime folklore and was often credited to Lapp (Sami) sorcery.
source: Nordic maritime folklore on wind magic

name: The Kettle of the Underjordiska
powers: Returned filled with gold, or borrowed at a price.
description: A pot or kettle that the underjordiska, the hidden people beneath the earth, were said to borrow from farm households. In Swedish legend a woman lends a kettle to the hidden folk and finds it returned filled with gold or a gift, or learns that borrowing from them carries its own price. The borrowed kettle is a common motif in stories of the underjordiska.
source: Swedish legends of the underjordiska

name: Kubbestol
description: A Norwegian chair hollowed from a single upright log, with seat, back, and arms carved from the same piece of wood, often decorated with chip-carving and floral patterns. Kubbestol chairs stood in farmhouses as the seat of honor and were even used as the bridal chair at weddings. They show the woodcarver's art also seen in stave church portals and seter crafts.
source: Norwegian folk furniture; museum collections

name: Karagoz
material: Dyed translucent leather (camel hide) on a stick
powers: Comic everyman of the shadow screen, bickering with Hacivat in plays performed behind a lit panel.
description: Karagoz, the shadow puppet of Ottoman Turkish theatre, a comic everyman who bickers with his friend Hacivat in the traditional play; the translucent leather puppets are worked behind a lit screen and the whole form takes its name from the main character, said to have been an ironworker whose antics amused the Sultan. A living oral-dramatic tradition of Turkey.
source: Turkish oral tradition and documented Ottoman shadow theatre

name: The Knot of Isis
powers: Guards the wearer through the power of Isis.
description: The looped red tjet amulet, the 'girdle of Isis,' worn by the living and the dead for the goddess's protection. Spell 156 of the Book of the Dead directs that it be made of red jasper and placed on the neck of the deceased so that Isis's might guards the throat. Red carnelian and faience tjets are common in New Kingdom burials, where they sit with the djed and ankh in protective groupings.
source: Book of the Dead, spell 156; amulet deposits

name: The Khamsa
powers: Deflects the evil eye and brings blessing to its bearer.
description: The open-hand amulet of the Maghreb and wider Middle East, called the Hand of Fatima after the Prophet's daughter and the Hand of Miriam in Jewish usage, hung in homes, worn as jewelry, and painted on doorways against the evil eye. The silver khamsa was the standard talisman of North African Jews and Muslims alike, with pieces from sheet silver to fine filigree set with coral.
source: Maghrebi ethnographic collections

name: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
powers: Said to command the wind and fell whole fields of grass; one of the Three Sacred Treasures.
description: The legendary grass-cutting sword drawn from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by Susanoo, then offered to Amaterasu and placed among the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia. Kept today at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, it is said to command the wind and cut down an entire field of grass in a single stroke.
source: Kojiki; Nihon Shoki

name: Kitsune's Crescent Comb
powers: Reveals a fox in human form; granting it service or love
description: The crescent-shaped comb that Japanese tales say a shapeshifting kitsune drops when its fox tail is betrayed. A man who finds one may gain the fox's love or service, and the comb recurs as the tell-tale clue in tales of fox wives whose disguise slips at midnight, linking the small hair ornament to the oldest fox legends of Japan.
source: Kitsune folktale tradition (Genjimonogatari imagery)

name: Khaen
powers: Voice of lam song and festival celebration
description: The free-reed mouth organ of Laos built from rows of bamboo tubes bound around a wooden wind-chest, its drone-and-melody sound the soul of lam folk song. Played at festivals, rituals, and courtship, the khaen is credited by Lao tradition with shaping the speech and poetry of the people.
source: Lao musical tradition

name: K'awiil Scepter
powers: Invests the ruler with the lightning-god's authority.
description: A short staff topped by a small figure of the Maya lightning god K'awiil, its mirrored forehead and snake leg identifying the deity, held by rulers in Classic-period stelae and murals as proof of divine kingship. Depictions at Copán, Tikal and Piedras Negras show it passed at accession, its serpent leg on the ground.
source: Classic Maya stelae and painted ceramics

name: Kachina Doll
material: Carved cottonwood root with paint and feathers
powers: Brings the blessing of the katsinam spirits to children.
description: Small carved and painted wooden figures of the katsinam, the spirit messengers of the Hopi, given to children to teach the identity and power of each being that visits the village from winter to summer. Carved from cottonwood root, the dolls are educational rather than worshipped, yet carry sacred meaning and ceremony. Since the late 1800s they have also become celebrated art sought by museums.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Katsina Owl Doll
powers: Teaches children the ways of the night hunter spirit.
description: A carved and painted doll of the owl katsina, one of the Hopi spirit beings that return to the villages in season, given to children so they learn the owl's wisdom and hunting power. Like other katsina tihu the doll is made of cottonwood root, its wings and face marked in the colors of the specific spirit. It belongs to the katsina carvings that carry the ceremonies' teaching into the home.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Kero
material: Carved wood, often with painted scenes
powers: Twin cups shared to seal alliance and honor the sun.
description: The paired ceremonial cups of the Andes, carved from wood as a flared goblet and drunk from in pairs at rituals of alliance, hospitality and the great festivals of the Inca calendar. Drunk together so each party shared the other's drink, twin keros sealed friendship. Colonial-era keros are painted with scenes of Inca life, a key record of how the empire remembered itself after conquest.
source: Inca-period and colonial keros in museum collections

name: Kultrún
powers: Carries the heartbeat of the land into ceremony.
description: The round drum of the Mapuche, its head painted with a cross and the four directions, struck by the machi, the ceremonial leader and healer, in rites and visions. Its beat paces the ngillatun ceremonies of thanks and the healing of the sick, and the drum is regarded as sacred, held in the machi's hands at the center of the ritual circle. The kultrún stands at the heart of Mapuche spiritual life.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Kayak
material: Sealskin stretched over a wood or bone frame
powers: Carries its hunter silently across the open sea after seals.
description: The one-man hunting boat of the Inuit, a frame of wood or bone covered with sealskin, so light and watertight that one hunter could carry it and paddle it alone across the open sea after seals and whales. The hunter sat in its cockpit, its deck lashed tight against waves. European explorers copied its shape, and the kayak entered the world's boats as a living Arctic invention.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic maritime records

name: Kente Cloth
description: Kente is the strip-woven silk-and-cotton cloth of the Asante and Ewe, assembled from narrow bands into bold geometric patterns, each with a name and proverb meaning. Weaving was a male craft tied to the royal court; colours and motifs encode rank, occasion, and moral teaching. Asante origin tradition credits the spider Anansi with inspiring the first cloth.
source: Asante oral tradition

name: Kuba Beaded Cup
material: Wood, glass beads, cowrie shells, brass studs
description: Ceremonial drinking cups of the Kuba kingdom of the DRC, carved from wood and densely covered with cowrie shells, brass studs, and glass beads in geometric patterns. Owned by Kuba kings and nobles, they were used in court ceremony and kept in the palace treasury; some cups take human or animal form.
source: Kuba court tradition; museum collections

name: Kuba Ndop Royal Figure
description: The ndop is a carved wooden portrait figure of a Kuba king of the DRC, seated cross-legged with the king's personal emblem (ibol) carved beside him. Each ndop commemorated a ruler's reign and was kept in a sacred house of the palace; the figure's gesture and pattern of scarification identify the individual king.
source: Kuba royal tradition; museum collections (British Museum)

name: Kalinga Royal Drum
description: The Kalinga is the most sacred of the royal drums of Rwanda, a decorated drum of the mwami's court that was beaten only at the most solemn ceremonies of kingship. Along with the court's other drums it accompanied the dances and rituals that affirmed the king's divine authority; after the monarchy fell, the original is said to be preserved abroad or in the national collection.
source: Rwandan court tradition; historical accounts

name: Kabyle Earthenware
description: Kabyle earthenware of Algeria is burnished, hand-built clay pottery made by Kabyle women in the Djurdjura mountains, shaped without a wheel and decorated with painted or incised geometric motifs. Cooking pots, water jars, and grain bowls served daily life; the reddish clay pieces are famed for their clean lines and remain a living craft of the Berber home.
source: Kabyle women's pottery tradition

name: Katar
culture: Deccan and South Indian martial culture
description: Push dagger of South India and the Deccan, held by its H-shaped grip and driven with a punch rather than a cut, a weapon of close-quarter combat and ceremonial display. Katars appear in sculpted panels of royal processions and temple walls, and the dagger's distinctive handle makes it an instantly recognised emblem of Indian arms in courtly art and museum collections.
source: Arms museum collections and temple sculpture

name: Khanda
description: Double-edged straight sword of the Sikh tradition, emblem of the Khalsa and of Sikh martial piety. The khanda also names the double-edged emblem that crowns the Sikh nishan sahib banner, and Sikh tradition holds the sword as a symbol of justice, truth and the duty to defend the defenceless, carried and honoured in Sikh religious life.
source: Sikh religious tradition and panthic practice

name: Kirpan
description: Curved sword or dagger that every initiated Sikh carries as one of the five articles of faith, a physical pledge to uphold justice and protect the vulnerable. Forged of steel and worn at the waist or in a shoulder strap, the kirpan is at once a religious obligation and a reminder of the warrior-saint ideal of Sikhism, never used without cause.
source: Sikh Rahit Maryada (code of conduct)

name: Kada Bangle
description: Steel bangle worn by Sikhs on the right wrist as one of the five articles of the Khalsa, a ring with no beginning or end that stands for the unbroken bond with the divine. Sikh tradition requires the kada to be worn with commitment to the Guru's path, and it is treated as a visible sign of faith, humility and belonging to the community.
source: Sikh Rahit Maryada (code of conduct)

name: Kandyan Crown
description: Royal crown of the Kandyan kingdom of central Sri Lanka, a jewel-studded, turban-like headdress that the last Kandyan king, Sri Vikrama Rajasinha, surrendered to the British in 1815. The crown and the rest of the Kandyan regalia are held today in museum collections and stand for the sovereignty of the highland kingdom and its court rituals.
source: Museum holdings and Kandyan court records (British Museum collections)

name: Kastane Sword
description: Sinhalese ceremonial sword with an elaborately carved handle, often a lion or demon head in ivory, worn at the waist for court dress and ritual. In Kandyan and low-country rites the kastane is used to invoke and control demonic spirits, and it appears in the exorcism traditions connected with the demon lineages of Sri Lanka, where the sword's presence is believed to command the unseen.
source: Museum collections and ritual ethnography (J Intangible Cultural Heritage)

name: Karahi
description: Deep rounded wok of cast iron or steel used across Pakistan to cook the spiced curry that shares its name, set over an open flame. In homes and bazaars the karahi is the daily vessel of celebratory and communal cooking, and its name has passed from the pan itself to a whole style of Pakistani dish served hot from the pan.
source: Pakistani domestic culinary tradition

name: Khukuri
description: Curved blade of the Gurkha warrior tradition, broadest near the tip, used for cutting, chopping and ceremony in Nepal. The khukuri is carried in its leather scabbard with two small companion knives, and Nepali folk belief holds that once drawn the blade should taste blood before it is sheathed again, a custom linked to its history as a war weapon.
source: Nepali folk custom and Gurkha regimental tradition

name: Khyber Knife
description: Straight-bladed knife of the frontier regions of Afghanistan and the Khyber, with a wide spine and simple handle, worn at the belt and used for cutting and defence. Named for the Khyber Pass, the knife is a familiar article of the Pashtun belt and appears in the material culture of the borderlands, carried for daily work and carried as a mark of the bearer.
material: steel, horn or bone handle, leather
source: Ethnographic collections of frontier weaponry

name: Kuchi Jewelry
description: Heavy silver ornaments of the Kuchi nomadic herders of Afghanistan, such as large necklaces, headpieces and bangles set with amber, carnelian and turquoise. Kuchi jewellery carries the wealth of nomadic families on the move, and its patterns echo ancient Central Asian styles preserved through generations of wandering life across the Afghan plains.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Kuchi material culture
